title: Autonomic Nervous System
memory_badge: Automatic control keeps internal organs working
think_prompt: Which body activities continue even when you are not consciously thinking about them?
definition: The autonomic nervous system coordinates involuntary activities of internal organs.
description: This subunit introduces the autonomic nervous system, its coordinating centres, its sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, and how these two divisions produce opposite effects to regulate internal body functions.
key_points: Autonomic nervous system|Involuntary control|Internal organs|Hypothalamus|Medulla oblongata|Sympathetic|Parasympathetic
image_description: 16:9 Grade 11 biology overview infographic showing a human torso with major internal organs such as heart, lungs and digestive organs, plus a simplified brain region. Use subtle nerve pathways to indicate automatic control. Visually split the system into Sympathetic and Parasympathetic branches without yet showing detailed effects. Clean scientific classroom-smart-board style.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify body activities that continue automatically without conscious control.
quick_check: What type of activities are coordinated by the autonomic nervous system?

title: Why Involuntary Control Is Needed
think_prompt: Why would it be unsafe if heartbeat, breathing adjustments and digestion required conscious control all the time?
definition: Involuntary control allows essential internal body functions to continue automatically.
description: Many internal organs must operate continuously and adjust to changing conditions without conscious effort. The autonomic nervous system provides this automatic coordination.
key_points: Automatic control|Continuous function|Internal organs|No conscious control
image_description: 16:9 educational visual showing a resting student while internal organs continue functioning automatically: heart beating, lungs breathing and digestive organs active. Use subtle motion cues and a small visual cue indicating that no conscious command is required. Clean realistic Grade 11 science illustration.
interaction_instruction: Ask students which internal functions would be difficult or dangerous to control consciously.
answer: Because essential internal functions must continue automatically without constant conscious control.

title: Internal Organs Under Autonomic Control
think_prompt: Which body organs need automatic nervous control?
definition: The autonomic nervous system supplies and coordinates internal organs that are involuntarily controlled.
description: Autonomic control is associated with internal organs such as the heart, blood vessels, respiratory organs, digestive organs and glands. The focus is involuntary regulation rather than voluntary skeletal movement.
image_description: 16:9 human-body infographic highlighting representative internal organs controlled involuntarily: heart, major blood vessels, lungs or airways, stomach and intestine, and glands. Keep the brain and nerve pathways simplified. Clearly distinguish these internal organs from voluntary skeletal muscles.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify which highlighted structures are internal organs under automatic control.
quick_check: What kind of organs are mainly controlled by the autonomic nervous system?

title: Coordinating Centres
think_prompt: Which brain regions help coordinate autonomic activities?
definition: The coordinating centres of the autonomic nervous system include the hypothalamus and medulla oblongata.
description: The hypothalamus and medulla oblongata act as important coordinating centres for involuntary internal activities and help regulate automatic responses through the autonomic nervous system.
image_description: 16:9 simplified sagittal brain diagram highlighting the hypothalamus and medulla oblongata. Add subtle arrows from these centres toward internal organs such as the heart and digestive system. Avoid advanced neuroanatomy and keep the focus on identifying the two coordinating centres.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify the hypothalamus and medulla oblongata on the simplified brain view.
quick_check: Name two coordinating centres of the autonomic nervous system.

title: Two Divisions — Sympathetic and Parasympathetic
think_prompt: Why would the autonomic nervous system need two divisions that often act in opposite ways?
definition: The autonomic nervous system has two main divisions: the sympathetic nervous system and the parasympathetic nervous system.
description: These two divisions often produce opposite effects on the same organs. Together they help the body adjust to changing conditions and then restore functions toward the normal state.
key_points: Sympathetic nervous system|Parasympathetic nervous system|Opposite effects|Internal regulation
image_description: 16:9 split infographic with a central human body and two large branches: Sympathetic on the left and Parasympathetic on the right. Use opposing arrows or balanced visual cues to show that the two divisions often act in opposite directions on the same organs. Keep detailed organ effects for the next scenes.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to name the two divisions and predict why opposite effects might be useful.
quick_check: What are the two divisions of the autonomic nervous system?
answer: The sympathetic nervous system and the parasympathetic nervous system.

title: Sympathetic System — Fight or Flight
memory_badge: Emergency → prepare the body for action
think_prompt: What changes would help the body respond quickly during an emergency?
definition: The sympathetic nervous system becomes especially active during emergencies and prepares the body for fight-or-flight responses.
description: During an emergency, sympathetic activity prepares the body for rapid action. Typical effects include increased heart activity, increased breathing activity, pupil dilation and reduced digestive activity.
key_points: Fight or flight|Heart activity increases|Breathing activity increases|Pupils dilate|Digestive activity decreases
image_description: 16:9 Grade 11 fight-or-flight infographic showing a person facing sudden danger. Around the figure, show clear organ-effect callouts: faster heart activity, faster breathing, dilated pupils and reduced digestive activity. Use arrows and simple icons, keeping the content physiologically clear but not overly detailed.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify which changes would help the body respond rapidly in an emergency.
quick_check: Which autonomic division is mainly activated during an emergency?

title: Parasympathetic System — Return Toward Normal
think_prompt: What should happen to body functions after the emergency has passed?
definition: The parasympathetic nervous system tends to reverse sympathetic effects and restore body functions toward their normal resting condition.
description: After an emergency, parasympathetic activity helps reduce heightened body responses and restore normal internal functioning. Its effects generally oppose those produced by the sympathetic system.
key_points: Restoration toward normal|Opposes sympathetic effects|Heart activity decreases|Digestive activity returns|Resting state
image_description: 16:9 educational before-and-after visual. Left side shows the body in a heightened emergency state; right side shows a calm resting state. Highlight slower heart activity, calmer breathing and restored digestive activity. Use a clear transition arrow labelled conceptually as return toward normal, without clutter.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to predict how parasympathetic effects should differ from sympathetic effects after danger has passed.
quick_check: What is the general role of the parasympathetic nervous system after an emergency?
answer: It helps reverse sympathetic effects and restore body functions toward the normal resting state.

title: Compare Sympathetic and Parasympathetic Effects
think_prompt: Can you predict one division's effect if you know the other division's effect on the same organ?
definition: Sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions often produce opposite effects on the same internal organs.
description: Compare the two divisions by their general role and representative organ effects. The sympathetic system prepares the body for emergency action, while the parasympathetic system restores functions toward the normal state.
key_points: Feature|Sympathetic|Parasympathetic;General role|Fight or flight|Return toward normal;Heart|Activity increases|Activity decreases toward resting level;Breathing|Activity increases|Returns toward normal;Digestive activity|Reduced|Restored/increased toward normal
image_description: 16:9 comparison-table visual with two equal columns headed Sympathetic and Parasympathetic. Use rows for General role, Heart activity, Breathing activity and Digestive activity. Add small organ icons but keep typography large and concise for smart-board viewing.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to state one opposite effect produced by the two divisions.
quick_check: What is the main relationship between sympathetic and parasympathetic effects?
answer: They generally produce opposite effects on the same organs.

title: Apply Autonomic Control
think_prompt: Can you identify which autonomic division is dominant from the body's responses?
definition: Autonomic responses can be classified by whether they prepare the body for emergency action or restore it toward normal functioning.
description: Use unfamiliar scenarios to decide whether sympathetic or parasympathetic activity is dominant. Increased heart and breathing activity during danger indicates sympathetic action; recovery toward resting conditions after the danger passes indicates parasympathetic action.
key_points: Emergency → sympathetic|Fight or flight|Recovery → parasympathetic|Return toward normal|Opposite effects
image_description: 16:9 assessment-style two-scenario visual. Scenario A shows a student suddenly frightened, with faster heartbeat, rapid breathing and widened pupils. Scenario B shows the same student calm after the danger has passed, with body functions returning toward normal. Label only A and B; do not print Sympathetic or Parasympathetic so students classify the scenarios.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify the dominant autonomic division in scenarios A and B and justify each choice.
quick_check: A person's heart and breathing rates increase suddenly during an emergency. Which division is mainly active?
